clue.text: Penning article, cancel dated book

indicators.note: to pen an animal is to shut it inside a fold, so one word closes round another

parts.note: to cancel an order is to annul it, and this word opens up to take a letter
the indefinite article is a single letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'dated' pulls towards old-fashioned, which is the trap; here it is literal, a book that carries a year on its cover.
explanation.definitionFit: dated book -> ANNUAL: a yearly volume for children or a trade, published once a year and stamped with that year on the front.

clue.text: See 25
Bathroom facilities spoiled bedsit

indicators.note: food that has spoiled has broken down inside, so the letters no longer hold the shape they were given

parts.note: a bedsit is a British single rented room with the bed and the living in it, and its six letters are the raw material

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sells a wrecked flat, which is why the six letters read as somewhere to live rather than as plumbing.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathroom facilities -> BIDETS: a bidet is the low basin for washing yourself, standard in French and Italian bathrooms, so the plural names fittings.

clue.text: Swindles bringing in very little money for troublemakers

indicators.note: to bring something in is to carry it indoors, so the small piece is set inside the big one

parts.note: a swindle is a scam, and the plural opens up between its last two letters
p is a penny, the smallest British coin, written after the figure as in 50p

explanation.walkthrough: 'bringing in' reads as income in the surface, which is the misdirection: it is an instruction about position, not about earnings.
explanation.definitionFit: troublemakers -> SCAMPS: a scamp is a mischievous child, so the word is affectionate where 'troublemakers' sounds stern.

clue.text: Unknown uniform seen in upsetting programme's medical episodes

indicators.note: what is seen in something lies inside it, so these two letters sit within the word that follows
to upset a thing is to tip it over, and a word tipped over is read from its far end

parts.note: a television programme is a series, and here it arrives tipped over
algebra calls an unknown quantity x, y or z
U is uniform in the NATO alphabet that radio operators spell with

explanation.walkthrough: Three conventions stack up in six words: the algebraic unknown, the radio alphabet, and a programme meaning a run of episodes.
explanation.definitionFit: medical episodes -> SEIZURES: a seizure is a sudden burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain, which is an episode in the clinical sense.

clue.text: Old German chancellor perhaps unaffected by revolution

indicators.note: spin the word through half a turn and it comes back identical, which is how a setter asks for a word that mirrors itself

parts.note: 'perhaps' marks a definition by example: one particular holder of the office, given by his first name rather than the surname everyone quotes

explanation.walkthrough: Bismarck, first chancellor of a united Germany, is the man being pointed at, and it is his forename the grid wants.
explanation.definitionFit: Old German chancellor perhaps -> OTTO: definition by example, since Otto von Bismarck held the office from 1871 and 'perhaps' admits he is one instance.

clue.text: Spirits chant with wings the wrong way round

indicators.note: a wing is what sticks out at either side, so a word's wings are the letters at its two ends
the pair swaps ends — what led now trails and what trailed now leads, while the middle stays put

parts.note: to chant is to sing, and it is this word whose two end letters change places

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' offers ghosts and the surface offers a choir; the drinks cabinet is where the answer actually lives.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirits -> GINS: gin is a distilled spirit, and the plural counts measures or brands of it, matching the plural definition.

clue.text: Woman from 25A doing a turn during gig that is occasionally lacking tricks

indicators.note: a turn takes a thing right round, so the name is read from its far end
letters that appear only occasionally are the alternate ones, and the rest are lacking — dropped from the count
what happens during something happens inside it, so those letters are planted within the others

parts.note: run the three words together and keep the first letter and every other one after it
the woman at the centre of the entry at 25 across is Ilsa, and she is turned round here

explanation.walkthrough: A clue pointing at another entry has to wait for that entry: 25 across supplies a name, and the rest of the letters come from words you can see.
explanation.definitionFit: tricks -> GASLIGHTS: to gaslight is to trick someone into doubting their own memory, after the 1938 play in which a husband does exactly that.

clue.text: Strangely iridescent rash

indicators.note: a thing done strangely is not done the usual way, so these letters do not stay in the order printed

parts.note: ten letters, and the only ten on offer — the giveaway that they are the raw material

explanation.walkthrough: 'rash' sits beside a word about shimmering skin, so it reads as the medical noun; it is the adjective meaning hasty.
explanation.definitionFit: rash -> INDISCREET: both describe acting without weighing what follows, though indiscreet narrows it to letting slip what should have stayed private.

clue.text: Arms on the counter somewhere in pub

indicators.note: to counter is to run against, so the letters are read against their own direction — right to left in an across entry

parts.note: arms in the military sense are guns, and it is these four letters that get turned

explanation.walkthrough: 'Arms' wants to be a pub name — the Queen's Arms — which is the trap; here it is weaponry, and 'on the counter' does bar-top duty in the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: somewhere in pub -> SNUG: the snug is the little partitioned room off the bar, quieter and traditionally pricier than the public side.

clue.text: Rooney's latest title with foreign team — one Zinedine Zidane oversaw originally

parts.note: Internazionale of Milan, the Italian club everyone shortens this way
'one' can stand for the speaker, the sense behind 'looking after number one'

indicators.note: what is there originally is what is there at the start, so each name gives up only the letter it opens with

parts.note: the footballer's two initials, which is also where the nickname Zizou comes from
the letter this verb begins with

explanation.walkthrough: Two famous number tens hold the surface together, but the Rooney who matters is Sally, and the title is her 2024 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Rooney's latest title -> INTERMEZZO: Sally Rooney's fourth novel, of 2024, borrows the musical term for a short piece played between two larger ones.

clue.text: Request from host exhausted religious viewership

indicators.note: an exhausted thing has had everything drained out of the middle, leaving only what was at either end

parts.note: the two letters left at the ends once the middle is gone
the same treatment on the longer word: outside letters kept, everything between them dropped

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration is the tell: four separate single letters means initials, and an invitation is the only set of four a host sends out.
explanation.definitionFit: Request from host -> RSVP: it stands for répondez s'il vous plaît, the French for 'reply please', printed at the foot of an invitation.

clue.text: Tricks Methuselah will use shortly … is one briefly taken in?

indicators.note: said shortly, a word is delivered clipped, and the letter it ends on never gets said
someone taken in has been let inside, so this pair of letters goes within the pair before it
the same instruction on a smaller word — say it brief and the last letter goes missing

parts.note: the compiler of this puzzle signs himself Methuselah, so he is 'I', and 'I will' contracts
the word docked of its final letter
two letters at face value, and they are about to be prised apart
the word with its tail cut off

explanation.walkthrough: Setters call themselves 'I' or 'me', so a pen name inside a clue is usually just a pronoun; the ellipsis is punctuation, not an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Tricks -> ILLUSIONS: an illusion is a trick of the eye or of the mind, so the plural nouns match — conjuring, not deception in general.

clue.text: Poem's outstanding when read aloud

indicators.note: reading aloud turns spelling into sound, so what matters is how the word beside it is heard

parts.note: a bill still outstanding is one still owed, and saying that word gives a different spelling of the same sound

explanation.walkthrough: 'when' does the joining and 'outstanding' is the only word doing any wordplay, which is why a three-letter answer needs so little of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Poem -> ODE: an ode is a formal lyric addressed to its subject, so the definition names the class this answer is an example of.

clue.text: One of The Wailers on the road with The Police

definitions.text: One of The Wailers on the road with The Police

parts.note: the capital letters push you towards Bob Marley's band; read small, a wailer is simply a thing that wails

parts.words: on the road with The Police
parts.note: the second band name does the same double duty — what travels on the roof of a patrol car is the thing making the noise

explanation.walkthrough: Two band names in one line make the surface read like a tour poster, and the capital letters are the whole of the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue is the definition: the wailing device that rides along the road with police, dressed up as a bill for two bands.

clue.text: No 10 tears into doughnut with bad reputation

parts.note: the two letters as printed, standing at the front

indicators.note: to tear into something is to rip your way inside it, so the piece before lands in the middle of the piece after

parts.note: a doughnut is a torus, the ring shape a circle makes when spun about an outside axis
written in figures, ten is a one and a nought, and those two shapes read as letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'No 10' reads as Downing Street, the Prime Minister's address, which is the trap; the two characters are being taken at face value instead.
explanation.definitionFit: with bad reputation -> NOTORIOUS: notorious means famous specifically for something bad, so the phrase swaps straight in as an adjective.

clue.text: Anxious sheep following that bloke

indicators.note: what follows comes along behind, so the animal's letters are written after the man's

parts.note: bloke is British for man, and the pronoun for one is two letters
a tup is a ram, a male sheep — a farming word British setters reach for often

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a field and a farmer; the answer is a mood, and the join between its two words falls in the middle of the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Anxious -> HET UP: het is an old past participle of heat, so someone het up has been worked into a flustered, agitated state.

clue.text: Some seethe as he strokes trophy

indicators.note: some of a thing is a part of it, and the part of a phrase a setter means is a run of its letters

parts.note: run the four words together and eight consecutive letters span them, starting inside the first word

explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the little urn England and Australia play their cricket series for, named after a mock obituary for English cricket printed in 1882.
explanation.definitionFit: trophy -> THE ASHES: the urn is the prize the two teams contest every couple of years, so the name stands for the trophy itself.

clue.text: Back in saddle, a pair of bachelors go out

indicators.note: the back of a word is its rear end, so only the letter it finishes on is taken

parts.note: the letter this word finishes on
B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in BA and BSc, and a pair means two of them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in the saddle' is a phrase the surface wants you to hear whole; the setter has split it, and 'Back in' is an instruction rather than idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: go out -> EBB: the tide ebbs when it goes out, so the definition is the verb in its tidal sense rather than leaving a room.

clue.text: A certain lady smiles when leaving M&S

indicators.note: what leaves goes away, so the letters named beside it are the ones that walk out of the word

parts.note: someone who smiles beams, which is the word to work on
the initials of Marks & Spencer, the British high-street chain, and the two letters that depart

explanation.walkthrough: A three-letter woman is nearly always a name, and this one is short for Beatrice; the shop is real, which is what holds the surface together.
explanation.definitionFit: A certain lady -> BEA: a woman's given name, short for Beatrice, so 'certain' does the work of saying one particular woman is meant.

clue.text: Attack dog's half-cut after two drops of beer

indicators.note: cut in half, so only the front half of the word survives — and half-cut also means tipsy, which is what the surface is selling
what comes after is written behind, so the halved word follows the two letters

parts.note: two drops taken off the top of the word beer
a setter is a breed of gundog, and half of six letters is three

explanation.walkthrough: 'dog' in a crossword is very often a breed and very often a setter, which is also the word a compiler uses for themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Attack -> BESET: to beset someone is to assail them from every side at once, so the definition is the verb in its harrying sense.

clue.text: Stuck-up old Stockholm-born actress failing to finish show off

indicators.note: stuck up the page — a down entry written upwards is read bottom to top, so the letters come out the other way
the word never reaches its end, so the letter it should have finished on is missing

parts.note: Greta Garbo, the Swedish star of silent and early sound films, born in Stockholm — her surname arrives a letter short

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck-up' does two jobs at once: haughty in the surface, and an instruction about which way a down entry is read.
explanation.definitionFit: show off -> BRAG: to brag is to boast loudly about yourself, which is what showing off is when done in words rather than deeds.

clue.text: Root vegetable, one of a group found among cabbages?
Make mummy different meal when doctor intervenes

indicators.note: made different means made other than it was, so these four letters do not stay in the order given
to intervene is to step in between, so the two letters land inside the rearranged ones

parts.note: the four letters of the word, reordered
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, the degree behind the title, and a standard crossword shorthand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Make mummy' reads as a family joke and is meant literally: the process named is the one that turns a body into one.
explanation.definitionFit: Make mummy -> EMBALM: embalming preserves a corpse with spices and resins, which is precisely the process that produces a mummy.

clue.text: Someone who's made-up about rare catch

indicators.note: things strewn about lie anywhere and everywhere, so the letters beside it are scattered too

parts.note: nine letters across two words, which is exactly the count the grid needs

explanation.walkthrough: 'made-up' looks like the shuffling instruction, and that is the trap — it is doing definition work, and the small word after it tips the letters over.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who's made-up -> CHARACTER: a character is a person invented for a story, and the phrase glances at a face made up with cosmetics too.

clue.text: Wax cylinder working after century, some hope?

indicators.note: what comes after is written behind, so this piece is added at the end of the other two

parts.note: C is a hundred, both the Roman numeral and the cricketer's hundred runs
a ray of hope is the smallest amount of it anyone can claim
a machine that is working has been switched on

explanation.walkthrough: 'working after century' invites you to put the switched-on word straight behind the hundred; it goes behind both other pieces, which the comma is quietly saying.
explanation.definitionFit: Wax cylinder -> CRAYON: a crayon is a short stick of coloured wax, so the definition names it by material and shape rather than by use.

clue.text: Someone badly missing school days

parts.note: read as longing: to miss something badly is to pine for it, which is the nostalgic grown-up the surface offers
read as absence: the same verb simply means not being there, and the days are what is being skipped

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue turns on one verb: 'missing' is either pining for something or plainly not being present, and only the second reading names a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines, on the second sense of 'missing': a pupil absent from lessons rather than an adult who pines for them.

clue.text: Spaniard's "house white" is port

indicators.note: the possessive tells you to take the two quoted words in the Spaniard's own language rather than in English

parts.note: the Spanish word for a house
the Spanish for white, in the feminine form the noun before it requires

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'house white' a wine list, which is the misdirection; the two words are meant one at a time and in translation.
explanation.definitionFit: port -> CASABLANCA: Morocco's largest city is its main Atlantic port, so the bare word names the class the place belongs to.

clue.text: After husband's in a better place, new squeeze?

indicators.note: a letter that is in something sits inside it, so the husband is planted within the word that follows
what is written after comes behind, so the final letter joins at the end of everything before it

parts.note: a better is someone who bets, and this is the place they go to do it
H is the standard abbreviation for husband, the one used on family trees
N is the usual abbreviation for new

explanation.walkthrough: 'a better place' reads as heaven, which is the trap: 'better' here is one who bets, and the widow the surface conjures is doing nothing else.
explanation.definitionFit: squeeze -> CASH IN ON: to cash in on something is to squeeze money out of an opportunity, the profiteering sense rather than physical pressure.

clue.text: Penny caught bouquet

indicators.note: to catch what somebody says is to hear it, so the word beside it is wanted for its sound and not its spelling

parts.note: a wine's bouquet is its smell, and the word for that smell said aloud loses nothing but a letter on the page

explanation.walkthrough: 'bouquet' is a wine's nose here rather than a bunch of flowers, and 'Penny' is a woman's name in the surface and a coin in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Penny -> CENT: a cent is the hundredth of a dollar or euro, and penny is what English speakers call the smallest coin of any currency.

clue.text: Player obsessed with technique knocked back whole band

indicators.note: knocked back means sent the other way, and an across entry read the other way runs from right to left

parts.note: the whole of something is its sum, and that word arrives here having been knocked over
a band is a ring, and a ring is written as the letter shaped like one

explanation.walkthrough: 'whole band' looks like one phrase about a group turning up complete; it is two separate words to translate, and only the first is turned.
explanation.definitionFit: Player obsessed with technique -> MUSO: British slang for a musician keener on gear and chops than on songs, usually said with a sigh.

clue.text: Transported upon sled, somehow fitting every other bit of globe in

indicators.note: somehow means by some means other than the obvious, so the letters arrive in an order nobody would predict
these extra letters are fitted in among the rest before the rearranging happens

parts.note: eight of the ten letters, in two small words the surface needs anyway

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a single letter, and every other one means only alternate letters are used along it

parts.note: skip the first letter and take the next, all the way along, and two of the five survive

explanation.walkthrough: 'Transported' offers a ride on the sledge, which is why it sits next to the sled; it is the figurative sense of being carried away.
explanation.definitionFit: Transported -> SPELLBOUND: someone transported by a performance is carried out of themselves, and being held by a spell is that state named another way.

clue.text: Travel stops Nordic people missing their capital

indicators.note: what is missing has gone, so the letter named beside it never appears at all

parts.note: the people of Finland, whose five letters are one too many
a capital letter is the big one a proper noun begins with, and the surface offers Helsinki to distract you

explanation.walkthrough: A country's capital is a city; a people's capital, printed, is the letter at the front. The clue leans on both senses at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Travel stops -> INNS: an inn is where a traveller breaks a journey for a bed and a meal, so the plural names them by function.
